name: table-layout-context
body:
A template that accepts tables receives its body's parsed tables in its layout context (template-context). Each table carries `headers`, `align` and `rows`: `.table.headers` is the header cells in column order; `.table.align` is the per-column alignments (`"left"`, `"center"`, `"right"` or `""` for none) in column order; and `.table.rows` is the body rows, each a list of cells in column order. A cell is a map with `html` — its inline-Markdown content rendered to HTML, with `{br}` as `
` — and `attrs` — a map keyed by the template's declared cell-attribute names, holding each attribute's value for the cell or nil when the cell does not set it (table-cell-attributes). `.tables` is the source-ordered list of the body's tables, and `.table` is the first of those tables or nil; the default `max_tables: 1` template uses `.table` (table-limits). The `table` and `tables` entries are always present: `table` is nil and `tables` is an empty list in a template that does not declare `tables` and in any body that carries no table, so a layout reads them without a guard. The context belongs to the template whose body carries the tables, at slide level and in every section instance it resolves. `.body` is the body's non-table content rendered to HTML: each table is omitted from `.body` and appears only under `.table`/`.tables` (body-rules), so a template renders its tables from the table context. A table's position relative to the surrounding non-table content is not carried; the layout places the tables it renders. `table` and `tables` are reserved top-level context names, unavailable as field or section names (requirements.constraint.reserved-template-names). AC: a layout reads `{{ range .table.rows }}`, a cell's `{{ .html }}` and `{{ index .attrs "highlight" }}`; `.table.align` gives each column's alignment; a template that does not declare `tables` still carries `tables` (an empty list) and `table` (nil); a body with no table gives `.tables` an empty list and `.table` nil; a body with two tables gives `.tables` two entries in source order; a table's position among the body's paragraphs is not exposed; a template declaring a field or section named `table` or `tables` is a templates error.
